title: The body, feeling ill, and giving orders
goal: Describe physical complaints at a pharmacy or clinic, then add **the command form** — which in Brazil turns out to be far simpler than the grammar books teach.
bekal: naming body parts and complaints with *estar com dor de*
giving commands and advice the Brazilian way
telling someone not to do something with *não* + the standard form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na farmácia
dialogs.intro: Budi walks into a pharmacy looking miserable. In Brazil, the pharmacist is often the first port of call for health advice.

lines.speaker: Farmacêutico:
lines.id: Good afternoon! Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Boa tarde. Estou com dor de garganta desde ontem.
lines.id: Good afternoon. I've had a sore throat since yesterday.
lines.literal: good afternoon. I-am with pain of throat since yesterday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Um pouco. E também estou com dor de cabeça.
lines.id: A little. And I have a headache too.
lines.literal: a little. and also I-am with pain of head.

lines.speaker: Farmacêutico:
lines.text: Toma esse aqui, de oito em oito horas.
lines.id: Take this one, every eight hours.
lines.literal: take this here, from eight in eight hours.

lines.speaker: Farmacêutico:
lines.text: Não precisa. Mas não toma de estômago vazio.
lines.id: No need. But don't take it on an empty stomach.
lines.literal: not it-needs. but not take of stomach empty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Got it. Can I take it with coffee?

lines.speaker: Farmacêutico:
lines.text: Melhor não. Bebe bastante água e descansa.
lines.id: Better not. Drink plenty of water and rest.
lines.literal: better not. drink plenty water and rest.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And if it doesn't get better?

lines.speaker: Farmacêutico:
lines.text: Se em três dias continuar, procura um médico.
lines.id: If it's still going on in three days, see a doctor.
lines.literal: if in three days it-continues, look-for a doctor.

notes: **Estar com dor de — the pattern you set up in unit 3, now used in full.** *Estou com dor de cabeça* (I have a headache), *de garganta* (sore throat), *de barriga* (stomachache), *de dente* (toothache), *nas costas* (backache). Notice that Portuguese says "I am with pain of head", not "my head hurts" — the body part isn't the subject of the sentence.

**Toma, bebe, descansa, procura — Brazilian commands use the *você* form.** Grammar books teach *tome*, *beba*, *descanse*, *procure*. But in everyday Brazil, people use the very same form as ordinary *você*. That's a huge simplification: you **don't need to memorize a command form at all** to speak.

⚠️ **Except when telling someone not to.** *Não toma* is heard in the street, but the standard *não tome* is more often used for prohibitions, especially by older people and in writing. Prohibitions are the one place where the standard form is still going strong.

**De oito em oito horas** = "every eight hours". The pattern *de X em X* is used for repeated intervals: *de duas em duas horas*, *de dois em dois dias*. It's a must-know formula if you buy medicine in Brazil.
**Melhoras!** literally "improvements", means "get well soon". It's the standard wish you'll hear from cashiers, drivers and strangers in the street the moment you mention you're unwell.

grammars.title: The command form: two tracks
body: The middle column is the one you **use**; the right-hand column is the one you need to **recognize**, because you'll see it on notices and in formal writing.
after: **For prohibitions, use the right-hand column.** *Não fale*, *Não coma*, *Não vá*. It's not an absolute rule — *não fala* is heard too — but the standard form sounds both firmer and more polite.
**Adding *por favor* turns a command into a fully polite request**: *Espera um pouquinho, por favor*. And an even gentler version uses *poder* from unit 9: *Você pode esperar um pouco?*
⚠️ Watch out for *vai* and *vem* — the two commands you'll hear most in Brazil. *Vai lá!* ("go for it!"), *Vem cá* ("come here"), *Vem comigo* ("come with me").

grammars.title: Giving advice
body: Formulas that are gentler than a direct command, and used far more often with people you don't know well.
after: **Melhor on its own is the most Brazilian formula of all.** *Melhor não* ("better not"), *Melhor esperar* ("better wait"), *Melhor você ir agora* ("you'd better go now"). It's short, warm, and doesn't sound bossy at all.
*Deveria* is the only advanced form in this unit; just learn it as a whole for *você* and *eu* — both are the same.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *As costas* is always plural, like *óculos* (glasses) and *férias* (vacation). *Estou com dor nas costas* = "my back hurts" — note *nas*, not *de*.
*O coração* is used for the organ **and** for feelings, just like English "heart". *Meu coração* is also a common term of endearment in Brazil, like "sweetheart".
⚠️ *A receita* means both **a doctor's prescription** and **a cooking recipe**. Context tells them apart, and the mix-ups are usually funny rather than dangerous.

**In Brazil, the pharmacist is the front line of healthcare.** For minor complaints, people go straight to the *farmácia*, not the doctor — and many medicines that need a prescription elsewhere can be bought over the counter there. The *posto de saúde* is the public health service, free for everyone, foreigners included.

What did he say? → *O que ele disse?*
Have you ever been to Rio? → *Você já foi ao Rio?*
